items.title: Analysis: Is Nvidia too big to fail? Its AI financing web raises the stakes
items.summary: The tech giant's web of ties to other companies is raising the possibility that it could do far-reaching economic and financial damage.
items.body: The swirl of sex-and-spying allegations around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is raising a worrying question: Could trouble at the chipmaker spread through the tightly connected financial network Nvidia has built to support the artificial intelligence boom? Serious problems with Nvidia could do far-reaching economic and financial damage. The company has made hundreds of billions of dollars in financial commitments to other firms to help the industry grow, earning it the nickname the "central bank of AI." The Federal Reserve and other financial institutions are closely watching the AI buildout to monitor for the possibility that an unexpected event could destabilize the global financial system. Even back in July Fed officials were discussing the possibility of of a "broad-based repricing of assets" in the event of problems in the AI sector.

items.title: Poundland set for more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
items.summary: The BBC understands the discount chain, which has been edging towards administration, will be given more time to find a buyer.
items.body: Poundland looks set to avoid immediate collapse after its US owners told MPs on Wednesday they were in favour of extending a deadline to find a rescue deal. The discount chain, which has 11,000 employees, has been edging towards administration after being blocked by Gordon Borthers from accessing cash in its bank accounts. A deadline to secure a buyer for the business is set to expire at midnight, but sources close to the situation told the BBC they expect more time will be given, thanks to the release of £10m in funding. A committee of MPs questioned Gordon Brothers following accusations that the investment firm hopes to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 stores and stock piecemeal.

items.title: Poundland owner extracted millions when chain was on ‘knife-edge’, MPs say
items.summary: Retailer’s management to seek two-week extension of legal protection from creditors in high court MPs have accused the owner of Poundland of extracting millions of pounds from the budget retailer when it was on a “knife-edge” as it seeks extra time to secure a rescue deal. The…
items.body: MPs have accused the owner of Poundland of extracting millions of pounds from the budget retailer when it was on a “knife-edge” as it seeks extra time to secure a rescue deal. The management of Poundland, which employs 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, will seek a two-week extension of legal protection from creditors from the high court on Thursday morning. The budget chain’s owner, Gordon Brothers, is under pressure to accept a bid for the company that would save retail jobs and protect thousands of suppliers. Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators two weeks ago. The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors until Thursday morning while a solution to its problems is sought. Directors of Poundland are now seeking a further 10 working days’ grace, which must be approved by the high court.

items.title: Is AIIB's complaint mechanism failing affected communities?
items.summary: The AIIB has a grievance redress mechanism for people affected by projects it finances. But those seeking to file a complaint face significant hurdles. Critics say reforms and greater transparency are needed.
items.body: For members of the Indigenous Sasak community on the Indonesian island of Lombok, the conflict over their land is not over. For them, a tourism and infrastructure project co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a source of frustration, as they believe it has led to the expropriation of their land and destruction of their livelihoods. In late September, they officially filed a complaint with the bank. It remains unclear whether this complaint will lead to an independent investigation. The AIIB, which finances major infrastructure projects across Asia, has a mechanism in place to deal with such complaints. Individuals who suffer adverse effects from the bank-financed projects may, under certain conditions, file a complaint with the institution. However, access to this process — known as the Project Complaints Mechanism (PPM) — remains controversial.

items.summary: With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging…
items.body: With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging international environment its companies have chosen to enter. On a weekday afternoon, the basement food hall of a central shopping centre was packed. Office workers queued for Chongqing noodles, while a different noodle joint from a major Chinese hotpot chain drew its own crowd. At opposite ends sat two restaurants specialising in fish: one founded in Shenzhen and the other serving the dish Sichuan-style. Across the aisle, a milk tea shop from Xiamen served iced drinks alongside a busy Luckin Coffee counter.

items.title: Jensen Huang affair in D.C.: Resignation calls and moves to tighten Nvidia China exports
items.summary: Huang was notably opposed to strict export controls on AI chips to China, which ruffled feathers with congressional China hawks.
items.body: Members of Congress are calling on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to resign, and momentum is building to subpoena the executive, whose company is a leader in advanced artificial intelligence chips. Senate banking committee member Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., doubled down Wednesday on his call for Huang to resign, and a key Democratic House oversight panel member and House Republican piled on. "As a matter of his own conscience, he should resign," Cramer told CNBC, in response to revelations that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy as the chipmaker he co-founded was given permission from the U.S. government to sell its technology to China. Huang, who leads a company that's been a chief beneficiary of the artificial intelligence boom, on Sunday admitted to having an affair with a woman whom news outlets have reported U.S. intelligence concluded was a Chinese spy .

items.title: Consumers are showing signs of strain even as they keep spending, CNBC/NRF Retail Monitor shows
items.summary: Retail sales rose at their slowest pace in nearly a year in October as American consumers showed signs of strain from high prices.
items.body: Retail sales rose at their slowest pace in nearly a year in October as American consumers showed signs of strain from high prices, according to the latest CNBC/NRF Retail Monitor. Total retail spending on a seasonally adjusted basis came in at $561.7 billion in October, a 0.2% increase from a month prior and 3.6% above where it sat a year ago, according to exclusive data released Wednesday. Core retail spending, which excludes restaurant spending, rose 0.3% month over month to $454.2 billion. Core spending was 3.4% higher than a year earlier. The monthly growth rate for total spending was the lowest since November 2025, an indication that shoppers are growing choosier as higher prices pinch pocketbooks. A strong Halloween season and an early start to holiday promotions kept the figure from being even lower, the NRF said.

items.title: Christmas toy rush being driven by squishies and building sets
items.summary: A bumper year so far for toy sales comes as debate intensifies over screen time and tech connectivity.
items.body: Traditional games, squishies and building sets are helping to drive a bumper year for toy sales, figures show. The data comes ahead of the crucial Christmas run-in for retailers, which peaks at 23 toys sold every second in the UK. The number of toys sold up to October was 17% higher than the same period last year and growth is at a 10-year high, according to research company Circana. The increase comes despite consumers' cost-of-living pressures, and there are signs that some of the biggest growth in sales is for toys priced between £5 and £10. Despite relatively low sales in recent years, the toy sector has been buoyed by sales to "kidults". The kidult market - which is toys and games for those aged over 12 - has been growing, particularly as adults buy toys for themselves. This growth has continued with a 22% increase in the value of sales in the first half of the year.

items.title: KKR and RWE are rich firms. Why do they need a UK state loan for their windfarms? | Nils Pratley
items.summary: National wealth fund is to lend £1bn towards the Vanguard projects – but whether the private equity giant needed help is debatable “This major investment in UK renewables is a vote of confidence for building in Britain,” declared the prime minister. Andy Burnham is obviously…
items.body: “This major investment in UK renewables is a vote of confidence for building in Britain,” declared the prime minister. Andy Burnham is obviously correct that the two Vanguard windfarms off the coast of Norfolk are huge investments . Together, they require almost £13bn of debt financing. But he can’t claim they represent a fresh expression of confidence. The project has been on the runway since the German utility RWE, the developer, was awarded a contract to build the windfarms in January’s renewables auction. Instead, the new news on Wednesday was how the project will be financed, which is where the story becomes interesting. On the equity front, RWE said it had sold a 50% share in the Vanguard schemes to KKR, the giant US private equity and infrastructure investor.

items.title: Taxing the rich? China’s offshore trust crackdown nets US$24 billion
items.summary: Personal income tax declarations linked to offshore trusts have topped 160 billion yuan (US$24 billion) since Beijing introduced new rules in late July tightening tax compliance – with October making up 75 per cent of the total, according to official data. The surge lifted…
items.body: Personal income tax declarations linked to offshore trusts have topped 160 billion yuan (US$24 billion) since Beijing introduced new rules in late July tightening tax compliance – with October making up 75 per cent of the total, according to official data. The surge lifted nationwide personal income tax receipts in October by almost 90 per cent, the State Taxation Administration (STA) said on Wednesday. The 90-day grace period for declaring personal income taxes related to offshore trust gains ended on October 22. Officials told state news agency Xinhua that most taxpayers had responded positively to the new requirements and that enforcement had delivered “notable” results. Taxpayers who filed inaccurate returns or remained non-compliant would be required to pay any outstanding tax, along with statutory late-payment surcharges, authorities said.

items.title: Canada’s ambassador warns Trump tariffs are driving up costs, threatening U.S. investment
items.summary: U.S.-Canada trade tensions persist as Trump's tariffs drive up costs, threaten investment and complicate negotiations between the two countries.
items.body: Canada's ambassador to the U.S. warned Wednesday that President Donald Trump's tariffs are driving up investment costs and discouraging business expansion, as new Federal Reserve research points to more price hikes for American consumers next year. "Uncertainty increases your cost of capital," Ambassador Mark Wiseman said at the B20 summit , a gathering of global business leaders in Washington hosted by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. "If you're going to build a new plant, add a new ship, spend money on R&D, the more certainty you have, the more likely you're going to do that," said Wiseman, a former BlackRock executive who became Canada's ambassador in February. His warning comes as Washington and Ottawa struggle to resolve a tariff quarrel affecting one of the U.S.'s largest trading relationships.

items.title: 'Not the answer': Labour MPs speak out against Rosebank as decision looms
items.summary: There is a growing expectation among senior Labour figures that drilling in the oil field will be given the green light.
items.body: Some Labour MPs have called on the government to reject the Rosebank oil field, saying it is "incompatible" with the UK's climate commitments. There is a growing expectation among senior Labour figures that drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland will be given the go-ahead. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that a decision would be "taken in due course" while Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh stressed that affordability of energy bills was her "overriding objective". But in a sign of the division within the party, more than a dozen Labour MPs expressed concerns in Parliament about approving it. Others expressed support, pointing to economic benefits. Supportive Labour MPs said some other parts of the world emitted far more greenhouse gases than the UK and warned of relying on imports.

items.title: Nvidia hires leading US law firm to investigate Jensen Huang’s relationship
items.summary: Move comes as chipmaker reels from reports its CEO was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy Nvidia has appointed a leading US law firm to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship between its chief executive, Jensen Huang, and an alleged…
items.body: Nvidia has appointed a leading US law firm to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship between its chief executive, Jensen Huang, and an alleged Chinese spy . The $4.1tn (£3tn) chipmaker’s board has hired New York-based Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz for the investigation, which will be led by the Wachtell partner Joon Kim. The firm’s website describes Kim, a former government prosecutor in New York, as a specialist in areas including internal investigations, white-collar criminal and regulatory defence, and crisis management. Nvidia did not give a timeframe for the investigation but the company has said Huang will continue to lead the business he co-founded “without interruption”. A committee of independent board directors, assisted by Kim and Wachtell, will oversee the investigation.

items.title: China’s shipyards overtake South Korea’s in LNG carrier market as demand surges
items.summary: China has overtaken South Korea in monthly orders for liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers for the first time, challenging its rival’s long-standing dominance in a high-value shipbuilding segment where demand is surging. The country secured five of the seven large LNG carrier…
items.body: China has overtaken South Korea in monthly orders for liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers for the first time, challenging its rival’s long-standing dominance in a high-value shipbuilding segment where demand is surging. The country secured five of the seven large LNG carrier orders placed worldwide in October, compared with just two won by South Korean shipbuilders, according to data from British shipping consultancy Clarksons Research. In the first 10 months of this year, Chinese shipyards secured 32 of the 76 large LNG carrier orders placed globally, while South Korean builders won 44. Global orders for new LNG carriers more than quadrupled from the same period last year, when just 17 vessels were ordered. China’s 32 orders represented a more than tenfold increase from its three orders in the whole of 2025, according to the report released on Sunday.

items.title: CoreWeave soars more than 24% for best day since April 2025 after strong Q3 report
items.summary: Neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN have come under scrutiny this month as investors assessed the sustainability of the AI trade.
items.body: CoreWeave shares jumped 24.71% Wednesday for its best day since April 2025 after the neocloud posted quarterly earnings that beat estimates and raised its guidance for the year. "Demand for the infrastructure is and remains overwhelming." CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Wednesday. "I think I said that we are 10x oversubscribed to the existing capacity that we have left in 2027, and we are multiples ... oversubscribed on the capacity we have out in 2028," he said. Neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN have come under scrutiny this month as investors assessed the sustainability of the AI trade. CoreWeave, in particular, sparked alarm when spreads on its CDS widened past 11% , generally viewed as a distress level, as investors have to pay up for protection against default.

items.title: Prime property, slow sales: why London’s stock of empty high-end flats is piling up
items.summary: Homes in the West End, Mayfair and Marylebone are going unsold – and developers are counting the cost London has no shortage of luxury flats. There are ultra-modern blocks in the most upmarket neighbourhoods – including Chelsea, Kensington and Mayfair – that offer marble…
items.body: L ondon has no shortage of luxury flats. There are ultra-modern blocks in the most upmarket neighbourhoods – including Chelsea, Kensington and Mayfair – that offer marble lobbies, concierge services and views across the city’s skyline. The problem for property developers is finding wealthy residents to fill them , leaving brand-new properties in London’s most desirable postcodes standing empty. In the capital’s zone 1 – which includes the City financial district, the West End and central areas such as Mayfair and Marylebone – there were 1,400 completed but unsold homes at the end of September, three times the number recorded in 2016, according to figures from the market researcher Molior. Just 1,600 homes started construction in the area in the past 12 months, 75% fewer than a decade ago, it found.

items.title: How China’s shrinking population is reshaping its education system
items.summary: China is planning to expand high school and university places while reducing class sizes in kindergartens and schools for younger students, as changing demographics fuelled by falling birth rates drive a shift in resources. The education system faces a dual challenge: fewer…
items.body: China is planning to expand high school and university places while reducing class sizes in kindergartens and schools for younger students, as changing demographics fuelled by falling birth rates drive a shift in resources. The education system faces a dual challenge: fewer young children are starting school even as larger cohorts of students enter senior high school and university, a senior official said. Huang Weiru, deputy director of the social development department at the National Development and Reform Commission, said at a news conference on Tuesday that the demographic shift called for downsizing some parts of the education system and a targeted expansion in others. The assessment comes as China frames education reform as part of a broader push to support high-quality economic growth with a shrinking population.

items.title: CoreWeave CEO Intrator tells CNBC he has canceled his planned share sale program
items.summary: After CoreWeave beat on revenue and upped its forecast, CEO Mike Intrator indicated the company will be fine despite last week's Democratic midterm sweep.
items.body: CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC on Wednesday that he has canceled his 10b5 stock sale plan after the company reported strong revenue growth and beat Q3 expectations . "Until there is a material change in in, in our equity pricing, my 10b5 has been sidelined," he told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." Under Intrator's 10b5-1 plan announced in November 2025, the CEO has sold 8.26 million shares at an average price of $96.14 per share for a total of $794.2 million. Intrator and his co-founders have faced criticism for their stock sales as the company's stock has struggled, with shares down 18% so far in 2026 despite a 20% post-earnings rally on Wednesday.

items.title: Air traffic control boss says he was ‘most disliked person in the UK’ after flight chaos
items.summary: Nats chief says he ‘quite enjoyed’ ignoring calls from Ryanair CEO to quit over system outages in September The boss of Nats has said he was “the most disliked person in the UK” after air traffic control systems failed twice in September, disrupting flights for hundreds of…
items.body: The boss of Nats has said he was “the most disliked person in the UK” after air traffic control systems failed twice in September, disrupting flights for hundreds of thousands of passengers. He told an aviation industry conference: “My name is Martin Rolfe, I’m the CEO of Nats – or as I like to think of myself, the most disliked person in the UK in September.” Airlines led by Ryanair called for Rolfe’s resignation after two technical failures in a fortnight at the two control centres run by Nats (National Air Traffic Control Services) stopped flights taking off and landing. However, Rolfe said he was “quite enjoying” ignoring the repeated calls from the Ryanair chief executive, Michael O’Leary, to quit. Airlines have said the outage on 8 September alone cost them tens of millions of pounds.

items.title: Japan and Vietnam are cooperating on critical minerals. Will it reduce reliance on China?
items.summary: An agreement between Japan and Vietnam to step up cooperation in critical minerals by tapping the Southeast Asian nation’s massive reserves could protect Tokyo from a slowdown in shipments from China, the world’s No 1 source of rare earth metals, analysts said, but replacing…
items.body: An agreement between Japan and Vietnam to step up cooperation in critical minerals by tapping the Southeast Asian nation’s massive reserves could protect Tokyo from a slowdown in shipments from China, the world’s No 1 source of rare earth metals, analysts said, but replacing China was “unrealistic”. During Vietnamese President To Lam’s visit to Tokyo this week, the two countries released a “joint vision statement” that said both countries had consented to “look into the possibility of identifying and implementing cooperation projects in critical minerals”. Japanese media outlets described Monday’s announcement as an acceleration of joint work in critical minerals, which are used in consumer electronics, electric vehicles and aerospace equipment. Japan, as a manufacturing country, needs them as factory inputs.

items.title: Fed's Goolsbee calls inflation report 'borderline disturbing' as central bank weighs more hikes
items.summary: The consumer price index rose more than expected in October, raising alarm among Federal Reserve officials.
items.body: Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee called the latest inflation data "borderline disturbing." "It's another distressing report — borderline disturbing," Goolsbee said in an interview with "PBS NewsHour " on Tuesday. "We've got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing," Goolsbee said. "We're going to have to deal with that." The consumer price index rose 0.4% on a seasonally adjusted basis in October, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Tuesday morning release. That was higher than economists had predicted, and the third straight month of outsized price increases. Goolsbee said he had not seen drivers of prices like tariffs fade over time like he had hoped. He also said continuously high inflation on services concerned him. And the Chicago Fed chief said lofty prices are a top issue for many people he meets.

items.title: Robot vessels take on the dangerous work of mine hunting
items.summary: The conflict in the Gulf is an opportunity for the US to test its autonomous mine-hunting systems.
items.body: Traversing the Strait of Hormuz remains one of the most dangerous trips a vessel can take. "To transit the Strait of Hormuz you need agreement between the captain and the crew to take the risk. You need war risk insurance. And the captain has to make the final decision," says Steve Cameron, a former merchant navy officer and maritime consultant. Missiles and drones are a threat from the air, but under the surface mines may also be lurking. "If you're a captain, you'd like to see evidence mines aren't present," Cameron adds. Modern mines rest on the seabed and detonate when they detect an acoustic or magnetic signal, triggering a pressure wave that will break the keel of a passing vessel. The technology itself is not difficult or costly, but the mere threat can stop a tanker fleet from sailing. Ian McFarlane of French defence group Thales is a naval architect who knows mine warfare well.

items.title: Labour MPs warn against weakening electric vehicle targets ahead of crunch talks
items.summary: Exclusive: Cutting 2030 goal would be a ‘step backwards’, say MPs, as ministers clash over proposed reductions Labour MPs are urging the government not to weaken its electric vehicle targets as divided cabinet ministers prepare for a crunch meeting on Thursday to thrash out a…
items.body: Labour MPs are urging the government not to weaken its electric vehicle targets as divided cabinet ministers prepare for a crunch meeting on Thursday to thrash out a compromise. Members of the climate and nature crisis caucus (CNCC) say ministers must not water down a legal requirement for carmakers to ensure that 80% of the vehicles they sell in 2030 are electric, saying doing so would be a backward step and “shortsighted”. The intervention comes as Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, prepares to meet the energy, business and transport secretaries to decide whether to change the target. A meeting planned for Wednesday has been pushed back to Thursday, according to government sources. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, wants to slash the target to 50%, while Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, wants to cut it to about 60%.

items.title: Bessent moved to military base amid 'growing threats' from Iran
items.summary: Bessent's role leading Operation Economic Outcast has made him one of the Trump administration's top targets of Iranian threats, The New York Times reported.
items.body: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has moved from his Washington home to a military base for his safety amid growing Iranian threats against him. Bessent's move, first reported by The New York Times and confirmed to CNBC by a person familiar with the situation, came as the U.S. war against Iran remains locked in an uneasy stalemate punctuated by intermittent fighting. Concerns about Bessent's security were heightened after The Wall Street Journal "published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located," the person told CNBC on condition of anonymity to discuss the nonpublicized move. The Journal published an aerial view of Bessent's $12.5 million Georgetown mansion in late January 2025, shortly after he bought it.

items.title: Kim Kardashian's Skims offers refunds for $148 advent calendar after backlash
items.summary: The contents of the calendar, including hair clips and keychains, have been widely criticised on social media.
items.body: Kim Kardashian's Skims is offering customers refunds for its $148 (£110) advent calendar which has been widely criticised on social media. The accessories advent calendar promised "twelve days of fun surprises" but has been mocked online for the quality of its contents, such as hair clips and keychains, with some comparing them to something you would find down the back of a sofa. A spokesperson for Skims has told a number of media outlets "for some, the calendar didn't meet expectations" and the company has "personally contacted every customer" to offer a full refund or credit to put towards other products". The shapewear and clothing business was co-founded by Kardashian in 2019 and has made the reality TV star a billionaire, according to Forbes magazine. Skims was valued at $5bn in 2025 when it raised millions of dollars in new funding.

items.title: Aldi cuts hundreds of UK head office roles as part of global cost trimming
items.summary: Supermarket’s move labelled ‘shortsighted’ by worker who calls upper management ‘woefully out of touch with reality’ Aldi’s UK business is cutting hundreds of head office roles as part of a global effort to trim costs at the budget grocer. The retailer is consulting with its…
items.body: Aldi’s UK business is cutting hundreds of head office roles as part of a global effort to trim costs at the budget grocer. The retailer is consulting with its technology team on the loss of up to 150 roles after 103 redundancies in its finance and administration team earlier this year and almost 20 more redundancies among buying directors. One affected worker described the cuts as “shortsighted” and said they showed that “upper management [are] woefully out of touch with the reality”. Jobs in stores have not been affected, although Aldi said it had reduced the number of regional managers slightly, affecting a handful of high-paying roles. The German-owned group is reducing the number of people in local country operations as it centralises more work.

items.title: Nvidia shares rebound as Jensen Huang faces scrutiny ahead of earnings
items.summary: Investors are assessing whether CEO Jensen Huang's affair will have spillover effects on Nvidia's business.
items.body: Nvidia 's stock rose 2.87% on Wednesday, after falling for two days amid the scandal that has rocked the world's most valuable tech company. Shares closed down 5.47% on Tuesday as more details were revealed about the impact of CEO Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy . They fell 4.3% Monday. On Tuesday, Nvidia announced it had hired law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate whether company secrets or national security were compromised. Huang tried to project "business as usual" as he returned to the office on Monday, people familiar with the matter told CNBC. The CEO was also in the office on Tuesday, conducting meetings, ahead of the company's quarterly earnings on Nov. 17. Investors are assessing whether the matter will have damaging spillover effects on the business.

items.body: The price of diesel on UK forecourts remains stubbornly close to October’s record high of £2 despite a sharp fall in oil prices. A litre costs an average of 197p, according to the AA, which described the situation as “dismal”. By contrast, petrol has fallen 6p to 168p from the peak of 174.7p in early October. That was the highest level since August 2022. High fuel prices are putting huge financial strain on households and businesses and Christopher Waller, a US Federal Reserve governor, told a conference in London this week that energy prices could remain “elevated”.

items.title: Meta head of infrastructure will leave and be succeeded by former AWS cloud exec
items.summary: Meta's head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering Santosh Janardhan will leave in 2027, with former AWS senior vice president David Brown taking over.
items.body: Meta's long-time infrastructure leader will leave the company in the new year, setting the stage for a recently hired former Amazon Web Services executive to oversee its massive data center technical operations. Santosh Janardhan, Meta's head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering, revealed his upcoming departure on Wednesday in an internal memo obtained by CNBC. Janardhan, who has worked at Meta since 2009, said "it's time to pass the baton" to former AWS senior vice president David Brown, who joined Meta in July from AWS. The executive move underscores Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg's efforts to expand the company's data center operations under newer leaders at a time of increasing investor scrutiny on capital expenditure spending by the social media giant and its hyperscaler rivals.

items.title: Clashes erupt in Barcelona after thousands join Spain general strike
items.summary: Tens of thousands of people have been taking part in the strike, called by the country's main unions over housing and the high cost of living.
items.body: Clashes have broken out between groups of masked men and police in Barcelona after tens of thousands of people took part in Spain's first general strike for 14 years, called by the country's main unions over housing and the high cost of living. Some 120,000 people joined a demonstration in the capital Madrid and more than 50,000 turned out in Barcelona, where footage showed masked men setting fire to rubbish bins and smashing shop windows as police fired tear gas. The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant." There was a heavy police presence in the centre of Barcelona on Wednesday evening, with officers wearing helmets and riot shields.

items.title: ITV to cut show budgets as UK TV and film production spend drops by more than £2bn
items.summary: Broadcaster plans to make £30m in ‘temporary’ savings before inquiry into takeover by Sky ITV plans to slash its programming budget as new figures showed that spend on the production of films and prestige TV shows in the UK was down more than £2bn over the last year. The…
items.body: ITV plans to slash its programming budget as new figures showed that spend on the production of films and prestige TV shows in the UK was down more than £2bn over the last year. The broadcaster plans to make £30m in “temporary” savings, including £25m in content and £5m elsewhere in the business. The announcement by ITV, which has agreed to sell its television and streaming business to Sky, came amid a backdrop of ditched commissions , falling advertising sales and job reductions in the TV and streaming industry . The Love Island and I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here! broadcaster said it expected ad revenues to fall between 5% and 10% in the crucial final quarter of the year, despite the typically busy Christmas season. Ad sales are expected to drop between 2% and 3% over the course of the full year, ITV said.

items.title: JetBlue unveils new first-class seats to bring back profits
items.summary: JetBlue gave reporters a look at its new first-class seats on Wednesday.
items.body: JetBlue Airways unveiled its new domestic first-class seats Wednesday as more of the country's carriers bet on the premium travel boom to make them profitable again. JetBlue announced it would offer a domestic first class — BlueFirst — in December 2024 and plans to start flying aircraft with the new seats and full on-board product next month. The carrier showed off the new cabin at its home hub at John F. Kennedy International Airport on Wednesday. Retrofits will continue during 2027, CEO Joanna Geraghty told CNBC late last month. JetBlue will have 12 of the seats on its Airbus A320 fleet and 30 extra-legroom seats, down from 42 of those options previously. Because the airplanes don't have ovens, JetBlue said it is offering an array of cold food options like sesame noodles, pastrami sandwiches and tortellini salad, though they vary by route.

items.title: Economies are improving, but rule of law is slipping. The buck now stops with Africa’s leaders | Kenneth Mohammed
items.summary: The west has spent decades judging Africa’s governance and colonialism is much to blame. But Mo Ibrahim’s latest index offers a different perspective – and some uncomfortable truths The west has never been short of advice on how Africa should govern itself. It has produced…
items.body: T he west has never been short of advice on how Africa should govern itself. It has produced rankings, attached conditions to aid and delivered lectures on corruption, often while its own banks and corporations have profited handsomely from the continent’s governance weaknesses. So, there was something refreshing about sitting in Cairo, listening to a Sudanese-born, self-made telecommunications entrepreneur and billionaire on why Africans needed to measure their own governments.

items.title: Singapore wants a bigger slice of the global gold market. Is it too late to the party?
items.summary: Singapore is stepping up efforts to become a key player in the global gold market, betting that vaulting service and tax incentives will help it attract flows.
items.body: Singapore is stepping up efforts to become a major player in the global gold market, betting that a new central bank vaulting service and tax incentives will help it attract more bullion flows. The Monetary Authority of Singapore on Tuesday launched a gold vaulting service for foreign central banks and sovereign entities, with an initial capacity of 500 metric tons. The city-state also plans to introduce tax exemptions for certain wholesale gold-related services such as vaulting, refining, recasting, testing and broking. In June, Singapore unveiled plans for a physical gold clearing system to facilitate the settlement of bullion transactions in the city-state, with operations expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027.

items.title: From blood group ID to cycle racks: I asked for little ways to fix broken Britain and the public’s ideas give me hope | Martin Lewis
items.summary: There are thousands of small tips to make our country better. People know what is wrong, and it’s clear they have solutions Have you ever come across an annoying little problem and thought, “why don’t they just fix that?” If so, I want to hear from you. I’m looking for your…
items.body: H ave you ever come across an annoying little problem and thought, “why don’t they just fix that?” If so, I want to hear from you. I’m looking for your ideas for practical, low-cost, non-controversial ways to improve the UK – whether that’s health, schools, transport, business, housing, policing, justice, tech, shopping, money – or owt else entirely. The spark for this happened just over a year ago, when I spoke at Politico’s fringe event at Labour’s conference. The key discussion was about Keir Starmer’s unpopularity. I was asked what I’d have advised the government when it took power, so I said : “Come up with 100 small things that piss people off and that you can fix, and they can see that you have fixed them.” Then I reeled off a list of small fixes for my subject area: the counterproductive way council tax debt is escalated; renaming “tax-free childcare”; and so on.

items.title: Investors pivot to defensive stocks as markets enter a ‘state of alert’
items.summary: Technology stocks have lost momentum while defensive sectors gain ground, as investors reassess risks.
items.body: Markets are in a "state of alert," according to analysts monitoring a pivot from riskier tech sector bets into defensive stocks. Technology stocks — a key driver of rallies in recent years — have been notably volatile in 2026. Concerns about artificial intelligence — particularly when it comes to capital expenditure, cash flow, debt and circular financing — have sparked multiple bouts of volatility this year. The Democrats' sweep of Congress in the U.S. midterm elections amplified pressure on the sector last week. Wall Street's tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index is up by around 8.7% since the start of the year as of Nov. 9 close, but gave up some of its year-to-date gains in October when it shed 5.3% over the course of the month.

items.title: What are cold weather payments and who can get them?
items.summary: Some people in England, Wales and Northern Ireland can get help with heating costs during cold spells.
items.body: As temperatures drop, heating costs rise, but there is some help for many households through cold weather payments. This financial help is triggered across hundreds of postcodes in England, Wales and Northern Ireland when there is a prolonged period of below-zero temperatures. In Scotland, those on low incomes and benefits may receive a separate winter heating payment, which does not depend on how cold it gets. The cold weather payment is a government benefit top-up to help with fuel bills , external . The average temperature in a local area must be recorded as, or forecast to be, 0C or below for seven days in a row. More than one payment will be made during the course of the winter if there are enough periods of cold weather.

items.title: For Trump, Musk and Farage, the message is the same: voters don’t want to be hijacked by billionaires | Rafael Behr
items.summary: A lesson from the US midterms is that electorates are repelled by the arrogant mega-rich buying democracy. This is a fight Labour can afford to pick For most people, $224m (£168m) is a lot of money, especially if you spend it and get nothing in return. But Elon Musk is richer…
items.body: For most people, $224m (£168m) is a lot of money, especially if you spend it and get nothing in return. But Elon Musk is richer than most people. In fact, there is no one richer. As the wealthiest of the US’s tech oligarchs Musk could afford to blow huge sums on a failed bid to prop up Republican candidates in Texas, his adoptive home state, in last week’s midterm congressional elections. He is reported to have spent a further $250m failing to engineer results in other races. His riches plausibly swung voters the other way in Texas. James Talarico, who last week became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 , made defiance of Musk’s meddling a rallying cry in his campaign. In political campaigns, as in other forms of marketing, it isn’t always easy to know what kind of spending moves the dial or how far.

items.title: Nvidia's Huang tries to project 'business as usual' in return to office after affair revelation
items.summary: Nvidia employees described the mood as "sad" as CEO Jensen Huang returned to the office after disclosing an affair.
items.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang walked into the chipmaker's Santa Clara, California, headquarters on Monday and conducted his regular morning meeting with top-level executives, people familiar with the meeting told CNBC. Huang kicked off the closed-door gathering by addressing his infidelity and sharing how sorry he was to his staff, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. They said Huang didn't take any questions and quickly pivoted to business and top agenda items of the day. The CEO was also in the office on Tuesday, conducting meetings just one week ahead of the company's quarterly earnings report. People inside the artificial intelligence chip giant said Huang tried to project "business as usual," even as the probe moved forward into his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

items.title: Growth at all costs is not a sustainable policy | Letters
items.summary: The key task should be to ensure that essential services improve the wellbeing of individuals and local communities, writes Peter Riddle . Plus letters from Sheila Triggs and Stephen Smith A key lesson for the UK from the US midterm elections is that a different approach to…
items.body: A key lesson for the UK from the US midterm elections is that a different approach to managing the economy is essential if Labour hopes to retain power in two years’ time. Voters in the UK will judge Andy Burnham’s government just as harshly as American voters have judged Donald Trump if they too feel the economy is not working for them. Meeting the rising costs of food, utilities, transport and housing has become a daily challenge for millions of people. The pain of rising costs is compounded by a collapse in the quality and reliability of many vital public services and a sense that many people feel that their community life has become more fractious, fragile and unsafe. Burnham, on becoming prime minister, discredited the previous 40 years of neoliberal economics because it had not delivered perceptible benefits for much of the population.

items.title: Mississippi Senate: Scott Colom lead over Hyde-Smith pops to more than 4,400 votes
items.summary: Tuesday was the deadline for provisional ballots to be resolved in Mississippi, and the deadline for the receipt of mail-in absentee ballots.
items.body: Democratic nominee Scott Colom on Wednesday significantly expanded his lead over incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi Senate election to more than 4,400 votes as the ballot count continued. That spread ticked upward slowly until just after 2 p.m. ET when a surge of newly counted ballots boosted his tally by 607 votes, and then soon after by another 621 votes. As of 2:30 p.m., Colom was ahead of Hyde-Smith by 4,404 votes, according to the Associated Press. With an estimated 99% of the votes in, Colom led Hyde-Smith by 49.18% to 48.72%. Independent candidate Ty Pinkins had 2.1% of the vote. Colom has steadily expanded his lead over Hyde-Smith for days as he has won a higher share of so-called affidavit ballots than he received in ballots counted on Election Day night.

items.body: Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives would have to raise the state pension age above 70 to meet the cost of keeping the triple lock, Treasury minister Torsten Bell has claimed. Labour has announced reforms to the triple-lock promise to come into force in the next parliament – with the initial proceeds earmarked for Andy Burnham’s national care service. The Conservatives have attacked the move, and insisted they would stick with the triple lock, which increases the state pension each year in line with the largest of inflation, 2.5% or earnings growth. However, Bell argued that with the costs of an unreformed triple lock increasing over time – to £50bn by 2050, according to government estimates – a Tory government would end up repeating the approach they took in the 2010s and speeding up planned increases to the state pension age.

items.title: AI datacentres plan on-site power stations on huge scale despite climate risks, research reveals
items.summary: 181GW of gas-fired capacity proposed for sites in US and Europe because of delays in connecting to national grids, says report Developers of AI datacentres plan to build on-site climate-destroying gas power stations on a huge scale to meet their energy demands, research reveals.…
items.body: Developers of AI datacentres plan to build on-site climate-destroying gas power stations on a huge scale to meet their energy demands, research reveals. Datacentres planned across the US, the UK and mainland Europe have proposals to build fossil fuel plants on-site to create 181GW of gas-fired capacity because of delays to connect to national grids, according to the findings. This is almost four times the total peak electricity demand of Great Britain. The research by BloombergNEF says this “speed to power” will – if the planned rollout happens – emit about 345m metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent a year in the US, where 90% of on-site gas-fired power stations are planned. This is equivalent to annual greenhouse gas emissions from about 72.8m fossil fuel cars.

items.title: CFTC investigates if Kalshi improperly self-certified event contracts
items.summary: News of the probe comes after the CFTC ordered Kalshi to take down a sports-related "mention markets" back in August.
items.body: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is investigating whether prediction market platform Kalshi failed to properly inform the agency of proposed event contracts, Kalshi confirmed to CNBC. Kalshi called it a minor issue in how the contracts were filed and said it is working with the CFTC to address the matter. The CFTC flagged weather-related contracts, Kalshi said. The leading prediction market platform didn't say when the agency began investigating Kalshi. The CFTC didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Politico first reported on the probe on Tuesday, noting charges could happen soon, based on the CFTC's private notification to Kalshi. The platform declined to comment on any possible charges. Prediction market platforms are allowed to self-certify event contracts without the federal agency's prior approval, as long as they comply with the Commodity Exchange Act.

items.title: Bank of England’s inflation response ‘risks higher interest rates for longer’
items.summary: Thinktank Niesr says timid rate rise last week likely to make inflation more persistent feature of UK economy The Bank of England is risking higher interest rates for longer after a hesitant response to rising inflation , according to leading thinktank. In a searing critique of…
items.body: The Bank of England is risking higher interest rates for longer after a hesitant response to rising inflation , according to leading thinktank. In a searing critique of the central bank’s tactics, the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (Niesr) said a timid increase in interest rates last week was likely to mean inflation staying above the Bank’s 2% target until at least 2030. The thinktank said inflation was likely to become a more persistent feature of the UK economy unless the Bank took tougher action . The Bank’s monetary policy committee increased the cost of borrowing from 3.75% to 4% last week and hinted at another increase to combat inflationary pressure unleashed by the Iran war.

items.title: WNBA Finals MVP Gabby Williams: 'Our existence is political'
items.summary: Golden State Valkyries star Gabby Williams speaks about winning the WNBA championship, being named Finals MVP, and the culture war over women's sports.
items.body: Golden State Valkyries star Gabby Williams doesn't expect the political and cultural issues swirling around the WNBA to go away anytime soon. Fresh off the Valkyries' first championship and winning the Finals MVP award, Williams spoke with CNBC's Alex Sherman about the league's place in those conversations. The WNBA has been at the forefront of several political and cultural issues this season, ranging from race to sexuality. "I think as a female athlete, just our existence is political," Williams said. "Being a female athlete just automatically becomes politicized because we're in a space where maybe we weren't welcome before." Williams said that she and many of her fellow athletes understand the fact that that playing professional basketball has brought them a larger platform.

items.summary: Bessent, driving force behind US push to cripple Iran’s economy, relocates over alleged threat to his life The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has relocated from his home in the Washington area to a military base after an Iranian threat against his life, the New York Times…
items.body: The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has relocated from his home in the Washington area to a military base after an Iranian threat against his life, the New York Times has reported . Bessent has spearheaded a US push to cripple Iran’s economy since the start of the Middle East war, vowing “economic asphyxiation” of the Islamic republic through a web of sanctions. He is one of a number of senior figures in the Trump administration including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and the new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, to leave their home to live on a military base or protected housing. The US national intelligence chief, Jay Clayton, said last month that Tehran had “substantially increased” its efforts to target Americans in the Middle East and beyond.

items.title: Zelenskyy warns Ukraine is 'not real estate' as experts say a Russia peace deal remains elusive
items.summary: President Zelenskyy warned Tuesday that his country "was not real estate," as a second and final day of U.S.-brokered peace talks got underway.
items.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that his country "was not real estate," as a second and final day of U.S.-brokered peace talks wrapped up. Speaking to reporters in Denmark late Tuesday, Zelenskyy said he was "happy" with what he was hearing from the peace talks in Abu Dhabi between Russian and Ukrainian representatives, but said he had been clear with U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner that "this is a country of our nation, it is not real estate." His comments come amid discussions on the future borders of Ukraine and post-war security guarantees, issues where the countries remain far apart. "Everybody is ready for dialog. First, stop the war in Ukraine. Second, security guarantees for Ukraine. Third, maybe some dialog about these topics of security," Zelenskyy said.

items.title: Developing countries in limbo as rich nations delay new climate finance plans
items.summary: Many governments are yet to set targets, leaving recipient countries struggling to plan and attract private investment Developing countries have been left in limbo by the failure of some of the world’s biggest economies to flesh out their plans for new climate finance. Poor…
items.body: Developing countries have been left in limbo by the failure of some of the world’s biggest economies to flesh out their plans for new climate finance. Poor countries are supposed to receive $300bn a year from the governments of industrialised nations by 2035, along with about $1tn from other sources, to help them cope with the effects of extreme weather and shift to a low-carbon future. But many rich governments have not yet set out their targets and plans for providing climate finance beyond the end of this year or next. This gap is damaging because it means recipient countries cannot plan and makes it harder for them to attract private sector investment to supplement the public sector money.

items.title: American soldier arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia
items.summary: The 41-year-old man is being detained in London under the U.K.'s National Security Act.
items.body: A senior soldier in the U.S. Army has been arrested in the U.K. on suspicion of spying for Russia, London's Metropolitan Police said on Tuesday evening. The unnamed 41-year-old man was arrested near Gloucester, a city in western England, on Tuesday as part of an investigation by the U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing. British police worked with U.S. authorities, including the military and the FBI, in their investigations. A senior NATO military official confirmed on Tuesday that the American service member was assigned to the military alliance's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC). ARRC, headquartered in the English county of Gloucestershire, is a 3-star NATO headquarters with more than 400 permanent staff from more than 20 nations ready to deploy land forces where they are needed.

items.title: US justice department sues Lyft over alleged refusal to serve passengers with disabilities
items.summary: Lawsuit filed in California claims drivers routinely refuse to transport individuals with service animals or mobility devices The Department of Justice sued Lyft on Monday, accusing the ride-share giant of discrimination for denying service to passengers with disabilities. The…
items.body: The Department of Justice sued Lyft on Monday, accusing the ride-share giant of discrimination for denying service to passengers with disabilities. The federal lawsuit, which was filed in the US district court for the northern district of California, said Lyft drivers have routinely refused to transport individuals who depend on service animals or use mobility devices, such as wheelchairs, an alleged violation of the Americans With Disabilities Act (ADA). In one example, provided in the complaint, a Nevada woman who uses a wheelchair, due to injuries from a near-fatal car accident, had a Lyft driver allegedly drive away, as she waved to catch his attention. A Texas man who has vision and hearing impairments began to leave his guide dog at home, despite the challenges of navigating, to avoid further service denials, according to the suit.

items.title: Mortgage rates jump sharply higher, after easing for four straight weeks. Here's why
items.summary: After falling for a month, mortgage rates jumped sharply higher on a hotter-than-expected inflation report.
items.body: Mortgage rates fell for four straight weeks, but that ended Tuesday, after a monthly inflation report came in hotter than expected. The average rate on the 30-year fixed mortgage rose 12 basis points from Monday to 7.30%, according to Mortgage News Daily. It was the largest one-day jump in more than a month. The consumer price index showed broad upward pressure on prices, not just fuel-related costs. This came after a monthly employment report Friday that also showed a more heated economy than analysts had predicted. "Given that the Fed explicitly said it was more focused on the inflation component of its job description at the moment (as opposed to the 'full employment' component), we were expecting today's data to carry far more weight than last week's jobs report. The reaction was logical an immediate," wrote Matthew Graham, chief operating officer at Mortgage News Daily.

items.summary: Industry experts pick out tiny turntable as one of their ‘15 hottest toys’ for the festive season A record player so small it belongs at a party in a Barbie Dreamhouse is one of this year’s must-have Christmas gifts as the vinyl revival takes an unexpected turn. The £19.99 micro…
items.body: A record player so small it belongs at a party in a Barbie Dreamhouse is one of this year’s must-have Christmas gifts as the vinyl revival takes an unexpected turn. The £19.99 micro music set plays dinky 1.5in records and comes with an exclusive “mini vinyl” of the school disco favourite APT by Rosé and Bruno Mars. The toy makes the Toy Retailers Association’s annual DreamToys list of the 15 “hottest toys” this festive season. The Mini Brands record player taps into the huge market for collectible toys. Part of the appeal is the 45 mini records to collect, ranging from Billie Eilish’s Birds of a Feather to Neil Diamond’s Sweet Caroline. The discs are sold separately in £8 “blind balls” with part of the attraction being the mystery of which songs are inside.

items.title: Measles is surging in the U.S. — and outbreaks can cost millions
items.summary: A new tool developed by Johns Hopkins researchers estimates that the 2025 measles outbreak in the U.S. carried an economic cost of more than $37 million.
items.body: Measles outbreaks aren't just a public health threat. They can also be a financial burden on the U.S. — and the cost could only deepen as the once-eliminated disease spreads more widely. The U.S. is expected to lose its official measles elimination status following a review by the Pan American Health Organization this week, after cases ratcheted to recent highs this year. More than 5,100 measles cases have been reported nationwide in 2026 as of early November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. Eight deaths associated with the disease have been confirmed by states so far in 2026: six in Pennsylvania , one in New York and one in Wisconsin . Based on this year's case count, a new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks.

items.title: Eisen by Guzel Yakhina — the man behind the montage
items.summary: A fictionalised biography of Sergei Eisenstein turns the Soviet film-maker’s life into a study of art, censorship and psychological torment
